result.answer:
Verdict: NOT ENOUGH EVIDENCE

**Evidence relevant to the claim (for):**
- The only paper in the directory on dogmatism reports that "users who engage on dogmatic comments tend to show increases in dogmatic posts themselves" [S:d394871083da#1].
- That paper does build statistical models of dogmatism from a Reddit corpus collected across conversational topics and annotated via paid crowdsourcing [S:d394871083da#1].

**Evidence against (the causal/randomized part of the claim):**
- The reported result comes from applying a predictive model to "millions of other Reddit posts" — observational text analysis, not a randomized intervention [S:d394871083da#1]. No span describes randomly assigning users to view dogmatic comments.
- The remaining papers in the directory do not study dogmatism at all: one covers multimodal named entity recognition (MNER) and the SnapCaptions dataset [S:cf73ee7b3729#1], the other covers STEP pre-training for document summarization [S:0fc8fd43b7f1#1].
- The only randomized procedure reported anywhere in these spans is a human evaluation on 20 randomly sampled documents ranking system summaries — unrelated to user dogmatism [S:0fc8fd43b7f1#5].

**Explanation:** The paper's finding is a correlational/observational association between engaging with dogmatic comments and subsequent dogmatic posting [S:d394871083da#1]. Nothing in the supplied evidence describes a randomized intervention that manipulated exposure and measured a resulting change in users' own dogmatism, so the causal claim as stated cannot be verified (nor refuted) from these passages.

citations.title: Identifying Dogmatism in Social Media: Signals and Models
citations.text:
We explore linguistic and behavioral features of dogmatism in social media and construct statistical
models that can identify dogmatic comments. Our model is based on a corpus of Reddit posts, collected
across a diverse set of conversational topics and annotated via paid crowdsourcing. We operationalize
key aspects of dogmatism described by existing psychology theories (such as over-confidence), finding
they have predictive power. We also find evidence for new signals of dogmatism, such as the tendency
of dogmatic posts to refrain from signaling cognitive processes. When we use our predictive model to
analyze millions of other Reddit posts, we find evidence that suggests dogmatism is a deeper
personality trait, present for dogmatic users across many different domains, and that users who engage
on dogmatic comments tend to show increases in dogmatic posts themselves.

citations.title: Multimodal Named Entity Recognition for Short Social Media
citations.text:

data such as tweets or Snapchat captions, which comprise short text with accompanying images. These
social media posts often come in inconsistent or incomplete syntax and lexical notations with very
limited surrounding textual contexts, bringing significant challenges for NER. To this end, we create a
new dataset for MNER called SnapCaptions (Snapchat image-caption pairs submitted to public and
crowd-sourced stories with fully annotated named entities). We then build upon the state-of-the-art

citations.title: STEP: Sequence-to-Sequence Transformer Pre-training for Document Summarization
citations.text:
Abstractive summarization aims to rewrite a long document to its shorter form, which is usually modeled
as a sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) learning problem. Seq2Seq Transformers are powerful models
for this problem. Unfortunately, training large Seq2Seq Transformers on limited supervised
summarization data is challenging. We, therefore, propose STEP (as shorthand for
Sequence-to-Sequence Transformer Pre-training), which can be trained on large scale unlabeled
documents. Specifically, STEP is pre-trained using three different tasks, namely sentence reordering,
next sentence generation, and masked document generation. Experiments on two summarization
